newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH-Howard's clever politics on native reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH-Howard's clever politics on native reconciliation.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard has played the most deft of political ploys at the National Reconciliation Convention on Aboriginal affairs in Melbourne today.

Howard managed to look generous to Aboriginal sensitivities on the heated issue of native welfare while still appealing to the apparently large number of voters tired of what they call political correctness.
His speech also reinforced his image as an honest broker standing between irreconcilable opposing sides in the native title debate.

Most importantly, the prime minister's tactics may attract some of the 10 percent of voters who, polls show, support the populist One Nation party of Pauline Hanson, which opposes Aboriginal welfare and Asian immigration.
Howard's manoeuvre worked like this:

First he explicitly apologised to Aboriginal leaders and supporters at the convention for the practice, abandoned in the 1960s, of welfare officers taking Aboriginal children away from parents whom they judged unfit.

Whether he would apologise or whether he wouldn't had been built up as a big issue before the convention: Such simple symbolism makes an extremely appealing story for the news media and Howard's known reluctance to co-operate with so-called political correctness made it doubtful that he would apologise.
But he did apologise, and that created the television footage of applause from the convention.

Howard's next step was to make one of those statements that drives a cleft between an interest group and the rest of the community: he simply stated that Australian history since British settlement in 1788 was not just a story of "imperialism and exploitation and racism".

Most Australians, even those unhappy about the appalling conditions in which many Aborigines still live, would find that statement unremarkable. One Nation supporters would certainly be very pleased to hear it stated.
But it attracted jeers from the convention and the spectacle of some of Aboriginal and political leaders turning their back on the prime minister.

When the story runs on the television bulletins this evening, many voters will perceive -- rightly or wrongly -- a generous apology from Howard followed by a refusal to be politically correct and then ungrateful jeers.
This is highly effective politics.
The scene will also reinforce the impression that neither side of the native title debate is happy with Howard so his policy cannot be too bad.
Many voters will remember that farmers jeered him quite aggressively when he spoke to them in outback Queensland on May 17.
Howard has published a vague draft policy to regulate native title in response to the High Court's extension of it in the Wik case in December.
The court ruled that, contrary to the assumption in existing government policy, local Aborigines might have unspecified rights to use land that had been leased to pastoralists.

This has upset farmers and miners on such leases in two main ways. Since the native title rights are unclear they do not know what rights are left to them. And whatever those rights are they will presumably leave them with less than they have now.
Aborigines, who have proposed a compromise, oppose any move to broadly cut back their entitlements to the land.
Neither side is satisfied with Howard's proposed policy.
